hub.title: From soil to market, deciding like a farm manager
hub.subtitle: Agribusiness management simulations for the Agribusiness program. Each mission runs a full season on a 3D farm that reacts to your decisions.
hub.disclaimer: Illustrative values for academic purposes. They are not technical recommendations or market quotes.

m1.title: Soybean: from soil to market
m1.text: Run a 100 ha summer season in Santa Cruz: 18 decisions, from the soil test to the sale.

m2.title: Corn and fertilization management
m2.text: Plan the nutrition of a corn field with a soil test and a tight budget.

m3.title: Sunflower and crop rotation

briefing.eyebrow: Mission AGRO #001 · Summer season · Santa Cruz
briefing.title: Your first soybean season
briefing.body: You manage the Los Tajibos farm, 100 hectares in Santa Cruz. Your goal is a profitable harvest: use inputs well, avoid losses from poor agronomic decisions and sell with a good margin.
briefing.how1: You make 18 decisions across six stages, from soil preparation to the sale.
briefing.how2: Every decision shows up on the farm and moves the budget, the yield and the crop condition.
briefing.how3: At the end you get your season report with a score from 0 to 100.
briefing.disclaimer: All costs, yields and conditions are illustrative academic assumptions, not technical recommendations or market quotes.

decision.overBudget: You exceeded the available capital by {amount}: the season needs financing that wasn't planned.

pestsFocal.title: Pest above threshold in one sector
pestsFocal.text: The follow-up scouting finds 13 caterpillars per meter only in the northeast sector: only that sector is sprayed.

pestsDamage.title: The pest spread
pestsDamage.text: With no follow-up, caterpillars defoliated the northeast sector and the crop condition dropped.

pestsBlanket.title: The spraying was not needed
pestsBlanket.text: The follow-up scouting shows the pest was under natural control in almost the whole field.

rain.title: Heavy rain
rain.text: 140 mm fall in three days. The field floods for a few days and machines can't get in.

rainErosion.title: Erosion on tilled soil
rainErosion.text: With no cover, the rain washes soil away from the tilled field.

rainRust.title: Rust spreads
rainRust.text: Humidity speeds up rust in the unprotected crop.

priceUp.title: Price goes up
priceUp.text: World markets rise: the local board price goes up USD {shift}/t, to USD {price}/t.

priceDown.title: Price goes down
priceDown.text: World markets fall: the local board price drops USD {shift}/t, to USD {price}/t.

log.title: Season log
log.start: Season starts: 100 ha and USD 65,000 of capital.

q01.title: Soil diagnosis
q01.scene: Before spending on inputs you need to know what your soil has.
q01.prompt: How will you diagnose the soil's needs?
q01.a: Repeat last season's fertilizer formula, which worked well
q01.b: Take samples and send them to the lab
q01.c: Copy the neighbor's plan, who had a good harvest last year
q01.fa: You saved USD 400, but you'll fertilize blindly: you may fall short or overspend.
q01.fb: The technician takes zigzag subsamples across the field and the lab returns pH, organic matter and available phosphorus.
q01.fc: The neighbor's field has a different history and soil: their recipe guarantees nothing on yours.
q01.learn: A representative test (0–20 cm zigzag subsamples, per zone) is the basis of all fertilization: it costs little compared with what it saves or earns.

q02.title: Fertilizer purchase
q02.scene: The lab report is in and the supplier is waiting for your order.
q02.prompt: The lab recommends {dose} kg/ha of phosphate fertilizer. Your field is {area} ha and each bag holds {bag} kg at USD {bagPrice}. How many bags do you buy?
q02.fa: 80 bags cover only half the rate: the crop starts with less phosphorus than it needs.
q02.fc: You bought 40 extra bags: USD 1,120 tied up in the shed with no yield benefit.
q02.learn: Rate × area = total kilos; kilos ÷ bag weight = bags. 80 × 100 = 8,000 kg ÷ 50 = 160 bags × USD 28 = USD 4,480.

q03.title: Land preparation
q03.scene: The field has residue from the previous crop and winter weeds.
q03.prompt: How will you prepare the land for sowing?
q03.a: Tillage with several disc passes, to leave the soil clean and loose (USD {tillage}/ha)
q03.c: Sow right away, without spending on checking weeds or the field (USD {rough}/ha)
q03.fa: The disc leaves bare soil: higher cost, less moisture and erosion risk if it rains hard.
q03.fb: The sprayer controls the weeds and the residue stays as cover: it keeps moisture and protects the soil.
q03.fc: You saved money, but weeds will compete with the soybeans from emergence.
q03.learn: No-till is the dominant system in Santa Cruz: it keeps moisture, reduces erosion and lowers costs, as long as the burndown controls weeds well.

q04.title: Seed choice
q04.scene: Three suppliers offer seed for your summer season.
q04.a: Uncertified, unknown origin: the cheapest on the market (USD {price, number, ::.00}/kg)
q04.b: Certified and adapted to the area (USD {price, number, ::.00}/kg)
q04.c: Good-looking, but with no germination or health test (USD {price, number, ::.00}/kg)
q04.fa: Cheap, but with no guarantee of germination, purity or variety: you start with fewer plants.
q04.fb: Guaranteed germination, health and variety identity, in a variety adapted to the summer cycle.
q04.fc: If germination is low, the stand will be thin even with the full seeding rate.
q04.learn: Certified seed is one of the most profitable investments of the season: it secures the plant stand and tolerance to local diseases.

q05.title: Seed calculation
q05.scene: You plan the sowing to reach the target plant population.
q05.prompt: Target: {population, number} plants/ha. Germination {germination}%, field establishment {establishment}% and thousand-seed weight {tsw} g. How many kg do you buy for {area} ha?
q05.fa: 4,000 kg only cover about 67 ha: the rest of the field stays unsown.
q05.fc: You have 4,000 kg left over and, if you overseed, plants compete with each other.
q05.learn: Seeds to sow = population ÷ (germination × establishment). Kilos per hectare = seeds × thousand-seed weight ÷ 1,000,000. Round up a little, without overdoing it.

q06.title: Seed treatment
q06.scene: The seed is ready. You still have to choose the treatment before sowing.
q06.prompt: Which treatment do you apply to the seed?
q06.a: None: the soil still has nitrogen from last season
q06.c: Replace the inoculant with urea, which supplies nitrogen faster
q06.fa: Without specific bacteria, the plant forms few nodules and fixes less nitrogen from the air.
q06.fb: The roots form nodules: the bacteria fix the nitrogen soybeans need, at almost no cost.
q06.fc: Urea costs far more, slows nodulation and does not replace biological fixation.
q06.learn: Soybeans get much of their nitrogen from biological fixation. Inoculating every season, with a compatible product kept out of the sun, is among the most profitable practices.

q07.title: Planter calibration
q07.scene: The planter is ready and the soil has good moisture.
q07.prompt: With rows {spacing} cm apart and {population, number} plants/ha, how many plants per row meter should you get?
q07.fa: Too few plants: the canopy doesn't close the row and weeds take the space.
q07.fb: Correct: 10,000 m² ÷ 0.45 m = 22,222 m of row per ha; 280,000 ÷ 22,222 ≈ 12.6 plants per meter.
q07.fc: Twice the plants: they compete for light, grow tall and weak and may lodge.
q07.learn: Row meters per ha = 10,000 ÷ row spacing (m). Plants per meter = population ÷ row meters. Plus a 3–5 cm depth, depending on moisture.

q08.title: Weeds in the field
q08.scene: At 28 days, weeds appear between the soybean rows.
q08.prompt: What do you do about the weeds?
q08.a: Wait: the soybeans will close the rows and smother the weeds
q08.b: Identify them and apply timely integrated control
q08.c: Spray whatever herbicide is in the shed, without checking registration or rate
q08.fa: Weeds grow and compete for water, light and nutrients right in the critical period.
q08.fb: With the species identified, control arrives on time and protects yield.
q08.fc: You controlled some, but a poorly chosen product injures the crop (phytotoxicity) and builds resistance.
q08.learn: The critical competition period is the crop's first weeks. Identifying the weed, using registered products and rotating modes of action prevents losses and resistance.

q09.title: Crop nutrition
q09.scene: Some plants look paler than others.
q09.prompt: How do you assess the crop's nutrition?
q09.a: Spray foliar fertilizer on the whole field as a precaution, before it gets worse
q09.b: Check nodulation and run a leaf analysis
q09.c: Stick to the plan: color differences are normal at this stage
q09.fa: You spent USD 2,800 on an application the crop didn't need.
q09.fb: The diagnosis confirms good nodulation: no correction is needed.
q09.fc: Nothing serious happened this time, but you missed the chance to catch a problem early.
q09.learn: Diagnose before you apply: a paler tone can be a cloudy day, poor nodulation or a nutrient. Measuring costs far less than spraying blind.

q10.title: Caterpillars on the leaves
q10.scene: Scouting finds defoliating caterpillars in one sector of the field.
q10.prompt: Sampling shows {found} caterpillars per row meter and the scenario's action threshold is {threshold}. What do you do?
q10.a: Spray insecticide on all 100 ha now, before the pest spreads
q10.b: Scout again and treat only above the threshold
q10.c: Don't spend: 8 caterpillars per meter don't justify any action
q10.fa: You sprayed the whole field with the pest below threshold: you overspent and killed beneficial insects.
q10.fb: The next scouting shows only the northeast sector passes the threshold: the spraying is targeted.
q10.fc: With no follow-up, the pest spreads and defoliates the affected sector.
q10.learn: Integrated pest management: scout, identify and compare with action thresholds. Not every insect sighting justifies spraying.

q11.title: Rust risk
q11.scene: The weather turns humid and Asian soybean rust has been reported in the region.
q11.prompt: How do you respond to the rust risk?
q11.a: Spray fungicide every week on the whole field to take no risk at all
q11.b: Scout and spray preventively according to risk
q11.c: Wait for symptoms on the crop before spending on fungicide
q11.fa: You protected the crop, but with twice the sprays and cost, and more resistance risk.
q11.fb: The drone maps risk by sector and the preventive spray arrives before the disease.
q11.fc: Rust spreads with the humidity and defoliates the crop before grain fill.
q11.learn: Asian soybean rust is the most damaging soybean disease in the region: scouting and a well-timed preventive spray are key.

q12.title: Harvest timing
q12.scene: The field is mature. The meter reads grain at {moisture}% moisture and rain is forecast in {rainIn} days.
q12.a: Harvest now, at {moisture}% moisture, before the rain arrives
q12.b: Wait two days for it to drop to {target}% and harvest
q12.c: Wait for the rains to pass to harvest fully dry grain
q12.fa: You harvested before the rain, but you'll pay to dry the wet grain.
q12.fb: Two sunny days bring moisture to the commercial range: you harvest on time with no drying cost.
q12.fc: The rain delays harvest: shattering and pod-damaged grain increase.
q12.learn: Harvest at physiological maturity with moisture near the commercial range (13–14%): not so wet that it needs drying, not so late that grain is lost.

q13.title: Production estimate
q13.scene: Before the combine goes in, you estimate how much you'll harvest.
q13.prompt: You sowed {ha, number} ha and the estimated yield is {yield, number} t/ha. How much soybean will you harvest (gross)?
q13.fbest: Correct: sown hectares × yield = gross production.
q13.fpoor: Check the math: sown hectares × yield per hectare.
q13.learn: Production = harvested area × yield. It's the base volume for planning trucks, storage and sale.

q14.title: Harvest losses
q14.scene: The contracted combine (USD {perHa}/ha) moves ahead and you see grain on the ground behind it.
q14.a: Keep going: with rain close, every hour of harvest counts
q14.c: Speed up to finish sooner and pay for fewer combine hours
q14.fa: You finished fast, but about 6% of the grain stayed on the ground.
q14.fb: With the machine adjusted, losses drop to about 1%.
q14.fc: More speed, more losses: about 10% of the grain was left in the field.
q14.learn: Every kilo that falls to the ground is lost income. Adjusting the combine and measuring losses with trays pays for itself.

q15.title: Transport to storage
q15.scene: The harvest must go to the storage center in {capacity} t trucks, at USD {tripCost} per trip.
q15.prompt: You harvested {t, number} t. How many trips do you plan?
q15.fbest: Correct: tonnes ÷ truck capacity, rounding up.
q15.fpoor: Poorly planned: trucks were short (pricier rush freight) or you paid for extra trips.
q15.learn: Trips = tonnes ÷ payload, always rounding up. A poorly planned trip costs more than an extra one.

q16.title: Grain conditioning
q16.scene: At the storage center, part of the grain arrives wet and with impurities.
q16.prompt: What do you do with the soybeans at storage?
q16.a: Store it as it arrived, to avoid paying for conditioning
q16.b: Clean it, measure moisture and dry if needed
q16.c: Mix wet grain with dry grain to bring average moisture down
q16.fa: Wet grain heats up and spoils: you lose about 6% of the volume.
q16.fb: Clean, dry grain: it keeps well and sells without discounts.
q16.fc: Mixing doesn't fix moisture: hot spots and discounts appear.
q16.learn: Post-harvest protects what you produced: moisture, impurities and temperature are controlled before storing or selling.

q17.title: Selling the harvest
q17.scene: The crushing plant makes you three offers. The board price is USD {price, number}/t.
q17.prompt: You have {t, number} marketable tonnes. Which offer do you take?
q17.b: Forward sale at USD {price, number}/t, with USD 1,500 of storage and financing
q17.fbest: You chose the offer with the highest net income after its costs.
q17.ffair: It's a valid, simpler option, but not the one with the highest net income.
q17.fpoor: It's the offer that leaves you the least: you get paid sooner but give up price.
q17.learn: Compare net income (price × tonnes, minus each option's costs) together with the risk and liquidity of each one.

q18.title: Season result
q18.scene: The season is over. Time to do the math.
q18.prompt: Revenue: {revenue}. Total costs: {costs}. What is your operating profit?
q18.learn: Simplified operating profit = revenue − costs. A later version adds financing, land rent, depreciation and taxes.

captions.briefing: The student runs a 100 ha farm in Santa Cruz, with limited capital and a profitability goal. The same farm changes with every decision.
captions.q01: First, the diagnosis: the technician samples across the field. Every decision shows on the farm and comes out of the budget.
captions.q02: Agronomy and math go together: from the lab's rate to the bags to buy.
captions.q03: The tillage system changes the soil you see, the cost and the erosion risk.
captions.q04: Choosing seed isn't only about price: germination and health define how many plants there will be.
captions.q05: Real agribusiness math: buy too little seed and part of the field stays unsown, visibly.
captions.q06: The lens shows what you can't see from above: the nodules that fix nitrogen.
captions.q07: The planter crosses the field, the rows appear and the crop cycle starts running.
captions.q08: Here we show a mistake on purpose: ignoring the weeds. It doesn't block the season, but condition and yield drop.
captions.q09: Diagnose before applying. Measuring costs far less than spraying blind.
captions.q10: There are caterpillars, but below the threshold. The right call isn't to spray the whole field: it's to scout again.
captions.q11: The drone builds the rust risk map and a rain event arrives. The season isn't the same in every attempt.
captions.q12: 18% moisture with rain in the forecast: a real trade-off between drying costs and grain losses.
captions.q13: Yield accumulates every earlier decision, including the weed mistake.
captions.q14: The combine harvests the field. If it isn't adjusted, lost grain shows on the ground and the volume to sell drops.
captions.q15: Logistics are calculated too: tonnes, truck capacity and trips to storage.
captions.q16: Post-harvest protects what was produced: cleaning, moisture and silos filling up.
captions.q17: A market event moved the price. The student compares each offer's net income, along with its risk.
captions.q18: The student closes the books of their own season: the question uses their numbers, not a memorized answer.
captions.result: The report connects agronomic decisions with the business result: costs, profit, score and where to improve.
